title: From Possession to Ownership: Land Law and the Treaty in Colonial New Zealand
author: Joe Davies

key_cases.name: R v Symonds
key_cases.relevance: Crown's sole and absolute right of pre-emption from Maori

key_cases.name: Wi Parata v Bishop of Wellington
key_cases.relevance: Treaty described as 'simple nullity' - now discredited

historical_timeline.event: Treaty of Waitangi signed by 500 Chiefs
FitzRoy allows direct land purchases, bypassing Crown pre-emption
R v Symonds establishes Crown's pre-emption right
Land Transfer Act introduces voluntary registration in England
Native Land Court established, begins assigning individual titles
Wi Parata case - Treaty deemed 'simple nullity'
Maori land holdings reduced from 60+ million to 7 million acres

content:
Chris Bevan states that 'land is much more than the sods of earth that comprise it...socially land gives us somewhere to live, somewhere to build a family, somewhere to be an active citizen, it provides the blank canvas against which we shape our lives and our businesses'.

In light of this quote it is important to consider how this blank canvas, providing peace and opportunity for our lives, is ultimately regulated through its title legal system, in checks and balances, documentation and processes providing legitimacy to the symbolic wax and seal. This podcast will briefly set out the historical development of land registration in England to provide context to the notion of a root of title in possession developing into a root of title in ownership. We will then analyse this notion with regard to New Zealand's early land jurisdiction, and explore the way in which land law is at the heart of the political economic development of the early state.

There are two different sets of law proving titles to land in England, conveyancing and registration. Registration is governed by the Land Registration Act 2002 (LRA) whereas conveyancing is governed by common law, equity and also the Law of Property Act 1925 and Land Charges Act 1972. Judith-Anne MacKenzie and Aruna Nair write that the initial reform from unregistered to registered land was born from cumbersome transaction processes that led to the belief that land was an inefficient and slow market.

The idea of a national register of deeds, modelled on County models of the early nineteenth century, were superseded by the more ambitious proposal to introduce a system of registration of title. Titles had more information regarding the estate than deeds had done. Initially it was a voluntary mechanism under the Land Transfer Act 1862, until the updated Act of 1897 introduced compulsory registration and London was the first area that introduced compulsory registration. The distinction between 'registered' and 'unregistered' land is that registered land has information regarding title to that estate that appears on a public register maintained by His Majesty's Land Registry. The LRA 2002 also governs a range of technical aspects including information management and regulations that do not apply to unregistered land.

Kevin Gray and Susan Francis Gray write that the idea of title relativity, rooted in possession of property or land, is a fundamental aspect of land and property law. This principle states that ownership persists as long as possession is maintained, valid against all but superior claims. Additionally, limitations exist on reclaiming dispossessed property, as seen in cases like Asher v Whitlock (1865-66) LR 1 QB 1 and Pye v Graham [2002] UKHL 30. Gray and Gray argue that possession remains an important concept of land law because it is one side of a duality between 'the empirical reality of behavioural fact and the official recognition of abstract rights'. They have also suggested that the LRA has committed us to a greater sense of 'absoluteness' of title than has ever before been conceived in English land law, through the stable root of title and that ownership solely constitutes the basis, and therefore the ultimate foundation, of property entitlement, rather than recognising possession as the root of title.

Stuart Banner states that by distinguishing between 'land' as the physical substance and 'property' as the conceptual framework governing rights to use land, we can observe in colonial New Zealand the imposition of two divergent property systems by the British and the Maori on the same land. These contrasting legal perspectives shaped each group's understanding of the other's actions, and as settler government power strengthened over the nineteenth century, they largely enforced an English property system on the Maori.

John White writes that prior to European influence on New Zealand, Maori traditionally distributed property rights based on function rather than geography, assigning them to individuals and families. While the English typically consolidated these rights within a singular geographical area. For example, one family might utilise the same tree for fowling, while another would gather berries from it and having the right to use one location didn't necessarily mean one couldn't possess use rights in other areas as well. The Maori did not have a written language and their land was inherited not from individual to individual but rather the hapu or the greater iwi / subtribe or the tribe, and distributed amongst its resources by rangatira / chiefs.

New Zealand was born in 1840, as The Treaty of Waitangi was signed by 500 Chiefs and a representative of Her Majesty Queen Victoria. The Treaty was made up of three relatively small articles and Ian Wards states that this was considered remarkable at the time as the Crown opted to acknowledge Maori land rights across the entirety of New Zealand, largely due to concerns that any alternative approach could embroil the UK in a costly war outnumbered by a battle hardened peoples.

The second part of Article Two states:

'The Chiefs of the United Tribes and the individual Chiefs yield to Her Majesty the exclusive right of Preemption over such lands as the proprietors thereof may be disposed to alienate at such prices as may be agreed upon between the respective Proprietors and persons appointed by Her Majesty to treat with them in that behalf.'

This article gave the Crown the exclusive right to purchase lands from Maori through representatives appointed by Her Majesty. This was challenged however in 1843, with the young colony facing financial trouble, when Governor Robert FitzRoy allowed settlers to buy Maori land directly, bypassing the Crown's pre-emptive purchase rights. Subsequently when Governor George Grey took office he decided to take a test case to the Supreme Court in 1847 to challenge FitzRoy's interpretation of the Treaty. The case was centred on an island in the Firth of Thames purchased by a settler called McIntosh from local Maori, arguing it nullified Crown's ownership. Governor Grey however granted the same island to another settler, Symonds as a Crown title. Chief Justice William Martin ruled in favour of Symonds and stated that 'the sole and absolute right of pre-emption from the aboriginal inhabitants vest in and can only be exercised by her Majesty, her Heirs and Successors.'

Banner writes that through the 1850's there were four major factors that led to a complete overhaul of the Maori possession in use system into the English root in title system; causing a transformation in the rights and fortunes of both settlers and Maori. Firstly the colonists believed that the English system of property rights incentivised productivity more effectively than the Maori communal system; they contested that individual ownership spurred improvement and development efforts. Secondly religion played a significant role, as settlers viewed the Maori 'underutilisation' of land as a violation of religious commands to cultivate and replenish the earth. Advocates for reform also argued that adopting English titles would weaken traditional Maori political structures and enhance integration with colonial governance. Finally colonists repeatedly linked civilisation with the organisation of property based on geographic space, equating individualised land ownership with progress and communal land holding with barbarism. They believed that adopting English-style land ownership was crucial for elevating Maori society and introducing civilising influences.

The overhaul came in 1865 when The Native Land Court was established by the colonial government. The court began to assign individual titles to Maori land. Most remaining Maori land was then sold to the English, either to individuals or their government. James Belich states that in 1800, the Maori owned over 60 million acres of land; by 1911, they owned only 7 million, much of which was not productive land. A few million acres had been confiscated by the colonial government after the mid-century wars, but the rest had been sold.

In 1877, the role of The Treaty and the supremacy of the English title system was well and truly established as Wi Parata, a prominent Maori farmer and political figure, challenged Bishop Octavius Hadfield in the Supreme Court over the Anglican Church's failure to fulfil an oral agreement with Ngati Toa whereby the tribe had given land to the church, expecting the construction of a school for their youth. However, the promised school was never built. Later on the church acquired a Crown grant for the land without the consent of the iwi. The court dismissed the case, with Chief Justice James Prendergast deeming the treaty irrelevant to domestic law, setting a precedent for future Treaty breach claims.

'So far indeed as that instrument (The Treaty) purported to cede sovereignty - a matter with which we are not here directly concerned - it must be regarded as a simple nullity. No body politic existed capable of making cession of sovereignty, nor could the thing itself exist.'

By the close of the century, Banner writes that the Maori found themselves stripped of the majority of their ancestral lands, along with their traditional land system of possession in use. An alternative framework for delineating land rights, that of title and ownership had supplanted the old order of possession in use. With their military and technological advancements, the British were able to impose a new governance structure and dictate the regulations governing land ownership and transfer. This development compelled the Maori to redefine their understanding of land to one centred around geographical demarcations.

In conclusion, Chris Bevan's quote from the beginning of the podcast highlights the multifaceted significance of land beyond the mere physical realm. It serves as the foundation for our homes and families, a canvas upon which we develop our lives and businesses. Recognising this, it becomes evident that the legal framework governing land ownership plays a crucial role in shaping our societies and histories. By exploring the historical evolution of land registration in England and the transition from possession-based to ownership-based titles, we have gained a valuable context for understanding New Zealand's early land jurisdiction.
summary: This essay traces the evolution of land law from possession-based to ownership-based title systems, comparing English land registration with colonial New Zealand. It examines how the Treaty of Waitangi's Article 2 established Crown pre-emption, how this was tested in R v Symonds (1847), and how the Native Land Court (1865) systematically converted Maori communal land rights into English-style individual titles. The essay culminates with Wi Parata (1877), where Chief Justice Prendergast infamously deemed the Treaty a 'simple nullity' - a position that dominated NZ law for over a century before being overturned by modern Treaty jurisprudence.
